ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A sequence of squares is made of identical square tiles. The edge of each square is one tile length longer than the edge of the previous square. The first three squares are shown. How many more tiles does the seventh square require than the sixth?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A sequence of squares is made of identical square tiles. The edge of each square is one tile length longer than the edge of the previous square. The first three squares are shown. How many more tiles does the seventh square require than the sixth?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The figure shows the first three squares made up of identical small square tiles. The first is a square with side length of 1 square tile, 1 tile in total; the second is a 2×2 square, 4 tiles in total; the third is a 3×3 square, 9 tiles in total. Then reason: The problem says that the side length of each square is 1 square tile more than the previous one, so the side length of the nth square is n square tiles, requiring n^2 square tiles. The sixth square needs 6^2=36 square tiles, and the seventh square needs 7^2=49 square tiles. The difference between the two is 49-36=13 square tiles.

Compute the sixth square as 6^2 = 36 tiles and the seventh square as 7^2 = 49 tiles. Subtract: 49 - 36 = 13 more tiles.
